subject: Linear Mixed Effects-type model using a user-defined likelihood (speed improvements)

messages.author: d0ff065a579e7203
messages.subject: Linear Mixed Effects-type model using a user-defined likelihood (speed improvements)
parts:
Dear group:

I am a new Stan user and I really it, especially the user defined functions.

My question is about efficiency of user-defined likelihood for linear mixed effects model (LME).  In my experience so far, Stan is very fast in sampling from "off-the-shelf" LMEs; however, in my current example, I want to sample from a user-defined likelihood.  I notice that Stan is a bit slow than usual (just a little bit).  

I am using a user-defined likelihood for the first time and I am not sure if I am coding the sampler inefficiently or such slowness is expected in my case.  I would really appreciate your feedback regarding my situation.

My model is the usual mixed effects model, i.e., for i-th individual

y_i = X_i  \beta + Z_i u_i + e_i and u_i ~ Normal(0, \Sigma),

where y_i is a vector in R^n_i, beta is the fixed effect parameter, u_i is the random effect with covariance matrix \Sigma, and e_i is the idiosyncratic error with variance \sigma^2.  My likelihood is the usual LME likelihood of \beta, \Sigma, and \sigma after marginalizing the u_i s raised to a power ('nrep' in the code).

I have attached the Stan code.  I have put the data below using 'dput' in R [please assign this to the variable 'simList'].  Of course, this is a toy example, so everything will be quick, but I would appreciate any pointers on vectorization or better sampling schemes.

Thanks in advance.

rstan code:

stanCode <- readChar("lme.stan", file.info("lme.stan")$size)
mdl <- stan(model_code = stanCode, data = simList, iter = 5000, warmup = 3000, chains = 1, thin = 5, seed = 123)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Linear Mixed Effects-type model using a user-defined likelihood (speed improvements)
parts:
Our advice for coding covariance priors for random effects is
in the regression chapter of the manual. Short answer is that you
want to move to a Cholesky-factor parameterization for both speed
and stability.

You can also just use 0 for meanFixef rather than making a vector
of copies of 0 --- Stan will broadcast the 0 for you automatically.

You don't need to define mu or covRanef as transformed params --- you
can move those into the model block as local variables because you
probably don't want to save them separately.

There's not much you can do about Stan's clunky block and segment
functions if you're coding up ragged arrays.

You can increase the regularization of correlations by upping the
parameter to the LKJ density --- that can help condition correlation
matrices (e.g., avoiding correlation 1 answers).

You can also look at what happens with sclRanef --- if those are
getting crazy big values, you can swap the Cauchy out for a normal
to keep things better controlled.

Finally, this line's very inefficient:

covY <- (zmat * covMat) * zmat' + stdErr * diag_matrix(rep_vector(1.0, rows(zmat)));

What you want (assuming zmat is symmetric) is

covY <- quad_form(zmat, covMat)

and

for (k in 1:nobs)
covY[k,k] <- covY[k,k] + stdErr;

The former does the gradients much more efficiently and the latter
avoids constructing a huge matrix and adding a bunch of zeroes (which
isn't itself so expensive, but it sucks up time in the gradient calcs,
which are more costly).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Linear Mixed Effects-type model using a user-defined likelihood (speed improvements)
parts:
Dear Bob:

Thanks for your helpful and detailed feedback. 

Especially, the following change made a huge difference:

covY <- quad_form(zmat, covMat)

and

    for (k in 1:nobs)
      covY[k,k] <- covY[k,k] + stdErr;

I did not notice any significant change by changing to the cholesky-factor parameterization; however, this may be due to the structure of my problem.

Much appreciated.
On Wed, Jun 10, 2015 at 2:02 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Our advice for coding covariance priors for random effects is
in the regression chapter of the manual.  Short answer is that you
want to move to a Cholesky-factor parameterization for both speed
and stability.

You can also just use 0 for meanFixef rather than making a vector
of copies of 0 --- Stan will broadcast the 0 for you automatically.

You don't need to define mu or covRanef as transformed params --- you
can move those into the model block as local variables because you
probably don't want to save them separately.

There's not much you can do about Stan's clunky block and segment
functions if you're coding up ragged arrays.

You can increase the regularization of correlations by upping the
parameter to the LKJ density --- that can help condition correlation
matrices (e.g., avoiding correlation 1 answers).

You can also look at what happens with sclRanef --- if those are
getting crazy big values, you can swap the Cauchy out for a normal
to keep things better controlled.

Finally, this line's very inefficient:

    covY <- (zmat * covMat) * zmat' + stdErr * diag_matrix(rep_vector(1.0, rows(zmat)));

What you want (assuming zmat is symmetric) is

    covY <- quad_form(zmat, covMat)

and

    for (k in 1:nobs)
      covY[k,k] <- covY[k,k] + stdErr;

The former does the gradients much more efficiently and the latter
avoids constructing a huge matrix and adding a bunch of zeroes (which
isn't itself so expensive, but it sucks up time in the gradient calcs,
which are more costly).

- Bob
